name: Model State Vital Statistics Act (CDC/NCHS)
note: The CDC/NCHS Model State Vital Statistics Act (1992 revision) is the template most State death-registration laws follow. Under it the funeral director files the death certificate with the State Office of Vital Statistics within 5 days of death and before final disposition, getting it to the attending physician within 48 hours of death, and the physician certifies the cause within 48 hours of receiving it; medicolegal deaths are certified by the medical examiner. The certifier, not the registrar, authorizes final disposition. Copies are limited to the family and to people who need the record to protect a personal or property right, and onward flows are by agreement or request: to NCHS, to other States, and to agencies that ask.

steps.title: Another physician at the institution may pronounce death
steps.who: When the certifier is not available to pronounce, another physician at the institution who views the body.
steps.summary: Where the person responsible for the medical certification is not available to pronounce death, another physician at the institution who views the body may pronounce it, attest by signature or an approved electronic process, and with the certifier's permission release the body to the funeral director.

steps.title: Informant supplies personal data to the funeral director
steps.who: The next of kin or the best qualified person or source available.
steps.summary: The funeral director obtains the decedent's personal data from the next of kin or the best qualified person or source available; the Act puts the duty on the funeral director, not on the family.

steps.title: Physician completes the medical certification within 48 hours of receiving the certificate
steps.who: The physician in charge of the patient's care for the illness or condition that resulted in death; if absent or with approval, an associate physician, the institution's chief medical officer or the autopsy physician, for natural deaths.
steps.trigger: Receipt of the death certificate, which the funeral director must get to the certifier within 48 hours after death.

deadline.text: within 48 hours after receipt of the death certificate (which the funeral director must provide within 48 hours after death)

steps.summary: The funeral director must get the certificate to the certifier within 48 hours after death, and the attending physician must complete the medical certification within 48 hours after receiving it, attesting by signature or an approved electronic process, unless the death falls under the State's post-mortem examinations act. If the cause cannot be determined in time, the certifier tells the funeral director and the certificate is completed later as the regulations provide.

steps.title: Medicolegal deaths certified by the medical examiner or coroner
steps.who: The medical examiner or coroner of the jurisdiction where death occurred or the body was found; which deaths are referred is left to the State's post-mortem examinations act.
steps.trigger: A death where inquiry is required by the State's post-mortem examinations act.

deadline.text: within 48 hours after taking charge of the case

steps.summary: When the State's post-mortem examinations act requires inquiry, the attending physician does not certify; the medical examiner or coroner determines the cause of death and completes the medical certification within 48 hours after taking charge of the case. The Model Act itself does not list reportable deaths or say who must refer them.

steps.title: Funeral director files the death certificate within 5 days and before final disposition
steps.who: The funeral director or person acting as such who first assumes custody of the dead body.

deadline.text: within 5 days after death or the finding of a dead body and prior to final disposition

steps.summary: A certificate for each death in the State is filed with the State Office of Vital Statistics, or as the State Registrar directs, within 5 days after death or the finding of the body and before final disposition. The Office runs the only vital statistics system in the State.

steps.title: Certifier authorizes final disposition
steps.who: The physician or medical examiner/coroner who certifies the cause of death; for cremation, an additional authorization from the medical examiner or coroner.
steps.trigger: Certification of the cause of death.
steps.summary: The funeral director must obtain an authorization for final disposition before burial, cremation or removal from the State. Under the Model Act it is the certifying physician or medical examiner who gives it when certifying the cause of death, on a form the State Registrar prescribes, so disposition is tied to certification rather than to registration.

steps.title: Certified copies to the family or to those with a personal or property right
steps.who: The State Registrar or an authorized custodian.
steps.summary: Vital records may be disclosed only as the Act allows. Certified copies go to the registrant's spouse, children, parents or guardian or their representatives, and to others who show the record is needed to determine or protect a personal or property right; copies showing the cause of death are further limited. Death records become public 50 years after the death.

steps.title: State furnishes records to the national vital statistics agency under agreement
steps.who: The State agency or Registrar, to the Federal agency responsible for national vital statistics (NCHS).
steps.trigger: An agreement with the Federal agency.
steps.latencyNote: may be furnished such copies ... as it may require; no time set (§ 23(f))
steps.summary: The Federal agency responsible for national vital statistics may be furnished the records and data it requires for national statistics, under an agreement that sets the permitted uses and the Federal support. The Act sets no cadence.

steps.title: Government agencies obtain records on request
steps.who: Federal, State and local governmental agencies, for use solely in their official duties.
steps.summary: Federal, State and local agencies may, on request, be furnished copies of records or data for their official duties. Nothing in the Act sends deaths to benefit or record-keeping agencies unasked.

steps.title: Interstate exchange of records by agreement
steps.who: The State Registrar, to the vital statistics office of the State of residence or birth.
steps.latencyNote: may, by agreement, transmit copies; no time set (§ 23(h))
steps.summary: The State Registrar may, by agreement, send copies of records to the vital statistics offices of the States where the decedent lived or was born. The Act sets no cadence; the agreement governs.

steps.title: Death posted to the decedent's birth certificate
steps.trigger: Registration of a death matched to a birth record.
steps.latencyNote: authorized to match birth and death certificates; no time set (§ 28)
steps.summary: To prevent fraudulent use of a dead person's birth certificate, the State Registrar may match birth and death certificates on proof of death and post the fact of death to the birth record; copies of a birth certificate so marked are marked deceased.

registrationDeadlineDays.note: Within 5 days after death or the finding of the body, and before final disposition (1992 revision, § 13(a)).

informantDuty.note: The funeral director who first takes custody of the body files; the next of kin supplies personal data.

medicalExaminerScrutiny.note: No independent review of certificates; deaths under the State's post-mortem examinations act are certified by the medical examiner or coroner instead.

electronicRegistration.note: The Act allows certification and pronouncement by an approved electronic process and filing as the State Registrar directs, but does not require electronic registration.

certificateAccess.note: Certified copies to the registrant's immediate family or representatives, and to others who need the record to protect a personal or property right; open after 50 years.

gaps: www.cdc.gov and stacks.cdc.gov refuse this client (Akamai "Access Denied"); they were left alone. The 1992 revision was read instead on ftp.cdc.gov, CDC's own file server, which serves the same mvsact92b.pdf (February 1994, DHHS Pub. No. (PHS) 94-1115) under /pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Publications/DVD/DVD_3/Misc/, alongside the April 1995 scan mvsact92aacc.pdf and the 1977 revision mvsact77acc.pdf. archive.cdc.gov (its Solr index at search.cdc.gov/srch/internet_archive/wcms_widget) has no copy; govinfo.gov, gpo.gov, regulations.gov, nlm.nih.gov and naphsis.org are egress-denied; federalregister.gov's API reads but holds no text of the Act.

The 2011 revision was not found on any official host reached. It is reported to have been approved by NAPHSIS but not published by CDC, so this file follows the 1992 revision; whether 2011 changed the 5-day/48-hour periods, disclosure rules or added electronic-registration requirements is unknown.

Corrections from the first pass (which had no text): the physician's 48 hours run from receipt of the certificate, not from death; the final-disposition authorization is given by the certifying physician or medical examiner, not by the local registrar; and the copy rule is a family-plus-personal-or-property-right test, not the phrase "direct and tangible interest", which does not appear in the 1992 text.
The Model Act defers the list of reportable deaths and the duty to refer them to a separate State post-mortem examinations act, which it does not reproduce.

The Act says nothing about the Social Security Administration or other benefit agencies; the State's EDR feed to SSA is federal law (42 U.S.C. 405(r)) and sits in us-federal. The optional bracketed § 27(c)–(d) monthly institution and funeral-director lists were not recorded as steps.

The NCHS Funeral Director's and Physicians' handbooks (hb_fun.pdf, hb_cod.pdf, hb_me.pdf) are also on ftp.cdc.gov in the same folder but were not used, since only the Model Act's own text was in scope.
